concepts.name: Punch-Marked Coins (PMC): Origins, Features, and Issuing Authorities
key_dimensions: Earliest coins in Indian subcontinent — Janapada vs. Imperial PMCs and distinguishing features
Materials used (silver, copper) and the absence of gold PMCs — UPSC trap on metal types
Symbols on PMCs (sun, six-armed symbol, hill, tree) and their interpretive debates — religious vs. royal
Mauryan state control vs. merchant/guild-issued PMCs — distinguishing imperial from pre-imperial series

concepts.name: Mauryan Coinage: State Monopoly and the Arthashastra Framework
key_dimensions: Kautilya's Arthashastra on the Lakshanika (examiner of coins) and Rupadarshakas (currency testers) — institutional overlap trap
Pana/Karshapana as standard silver unit — weight standards and debasement penalties described in Arthashastra
Absence of gold coins in Mauryan period — contrast with later Gupta gold coinage (common UPSC confusion)
Counterfeit coin punishment under Arthashastra vs. actual archaeological evidence of coin standardization

concepts.name: Indo-Greek Coinage: Bilingual, Bimetallic, and Portraiture Innovations
key_dimensions: First rulers in India to issue coins with portraits — significance for numismatic dating methodology
Bilingual legends (Greek on obverse, Kharosthi/Brahmi on reverse) — cultural syncretism evidence
Introduction of nickel coins by Indo-Greeks — rare metal use, UPSC trap on 'first use of nickel'
Menander I (Milinda) coins — Buddhist symbolism and the Milindapanha connection

concepts.name: Saka-Kshatrapa Coinage: Regional Variation and Administrative Significance
key_dimensions: Western Kshatrapas using silver coins with regnal years — earliest dated coins in India, UPSC trap
Bilingual legends continuing Indo-Greek tradition vs. gradual Indianization of iconography
Lead coins of Satavahanas vs. silver coins of Western Kshatrapas — material contrast in same period
Kshatrapa coins as historical source for reconstructing dynastic genealogy — numismatics as historiography

concepts.name: Kushana Coinage: Gold Standard, Dynastic Legitimacy, and Religious Syncretism
key_dimensions: Kushanas introducing large-scale gold coinage (Dinara) — contrast with Mauryan absence of gold coins
Devalued gold standard compared to Roman Aureus — trade implications with Rome and bullion drain debate
Pantheon of gods on Kushana coins: Greek (Helios), Iranian (Mithra), Indian (Shiva, Buddha) — religious syncretism evidence
BACTRIAN Greek script on Kanishka I's coins replaced by a Kushana script — script innovation trap
Coins as evidence for Kanishka's date — the unresolved historiographical controversy

concepts.name: Satavahana Coinage: Lead Coins, Regional Economy, and Deccan Trade
key_dimensions: Satavahanas as first major dynasty to use lead coins — significance for base-metal economy in Deccan
Potin (copper-tin alloy) and silver coins alongside lead — multi-metal coinage system
Bilingual coins (Brahmi and Prakrit) — Satavahana coins as source for dynastic names (Gautamiputra, Vasisthiputra)
Contrast with contemporary Kshatrapa silver coins — reflects different economic zones in peninsular India

concepts.name: Gupta Coinage: Gold Dinaras, Iconographic Richness, and Economic Apogee
key_dimensions: Gupta gold coins (Dinaras) — highest gold purity in ancient India, symbolizing economic prosperity
Eight coin types of Chandragupta II — Archer, Horseman, Lion-slayer types and their iconographic meaning
Progressive debasement of Gupta gold coins in later period — indicator of economic decline and UPSC trap
Silver coins introduced by Chandragupta II after defeating Western Kshatrapas — administrative assimilation evidence
Absence of Gupta copper coins in early phase vs. later copper issues — economic interpretation debate

concepts.name: Roman Coins in India: Trade Imbalance, Hoards, and Pliny's Lament
key_dimensions: Roman gold and silver coin hoards concentrated in South India (Tamil Nadu, Kerala) — spice/silk trade evidence
Pliny's complaint of gold drain to India (Natural History) — Roman perspective on trade deficit
Defacement/countermarking of Roman coins in India — indicates use as bullion rather than currency
Contrast between Roman coin distribution in South India vs. Kushana coins in North India — two trade circuit zones

concepts.name: Tamil Sangam-Period Coinage: Indigenous Tradition and Trade Tokens
key_dimensions: Punch-marked coins of early Tamil kingdoms vs. later die-struck coins — transition in South India
Coins of Pandyas, Cheras, Cholas — symbols (fish, bow, tiger) as dynastic emblems on coins
Sangam literature references to currency (Kasu) — literary corroboration of numismatic evidence
Overlap and distinction between indigenous Tamil coins and Roman coin circulation in same region

concepts.name: Coin Metallurgy and Debasement: Economic Indicator Across Dynasties
key_dimensions: Progressive debasement from Kushana to later Gupta — relationship between debasement and political decline
Satavahana lead coinage as adaptation to metal scarcity vs. Kushana gold abundance — regional resource explanation
Arthashastra's prescribed alloy ratios for coins — theoretical standard vs. actual practice
Debasement as UPSC trap: Post-Gupta coinage debasement often confused with Kushana debasement timeline

concepts.name: Coin Iconography as Historical Source: Religion, Royalty, and Legitimacy
key_dimensions: Coins as primary source for religious affiliation of rulers — Shaivism (Kushana), Vaishnavism (Gupta), Buddhism
Royal portraiture evolution: Indo-Greek realistic portraits vs. stylized Indian representations
Lakshmi/Goddess imagery on Gupta coins — legitimizing royal authority through divine association
UPSC trap: Coins NOT showing religious affiliation — Mauryan PMCs lack religious symbols, inference limitations

concepts.name: Weight Standards and Metrological Systems Across Dynasties
key_dimensions: Karshapana (Mauryan) vs. Suvarna/Nishka (Vedic references) vs. Dinara (Gupta) — weight unit evolution
Arthashastra's detailed weight system (Ratti, Masa, Pala, Dharana) — standardization mechanism
Kushana Dinara weight (8 grams) matching Roman Aureus — deliberate synchronization for trade
Inconsistency between Arthashastra prescriptions and actual excavated coin weights — historiographical problem

concepts.name: Coinage and Guild (Shreni) Economy: Private vs. State Minting
key_dimensions: Guild-issued coins (Takshashila, Mathura guilds) — evidence for private minting authority in ancient India
Lead tokens and copper coins issued by guilds — functional difference from state coinage
Arthashastra's regulation of private coin issuers — tension between state monopoly and guild autonomy
Gupta period guild coins alongside royal coins — parallel monetary systems and UPSC trap on 'only state minted'

concepts.name: Post-Gupta and Early Medieval Coinage: Decline, Continuity, and Regional Fragmentation
key_dimensions: Near disappearance of gold coinage after Gupta decline — 'Dark Age' of Indian numismatics debate
Rise of regional coinage: Gurjara-Pratihara, Rashtrakuta, Pala coins — fragmentation reflecting political disintegration
Continuation of Gupta iconographic traditions in post-Gupta dynastic coins — cultural continuity vs. political rupture
Harsha's coinage — extremely rare, debate about whether he issued coins at all (UPSC trap)

concepts.name: Coins as Evidence for Indo-Roman Trade: Pepper, Silk, and the Bullion Debate
key_dimensions: Stratigraphic distribution of Roman coins in South Indian sites (Arikamedu, Karur, Coimbatore hoard) — trade route mapping
Debate: Were Roman coins used as currency or melted for bullion in India? — implication for monetization levels
Decline of Roman coin import after 3rd century CE crisis — correlation with Sangam literature's 'end of golden age'
Kushana coins filling the vacuum in North India while Roman coins circulate in South — dual monetary spheres

concepts.name: Coin Legends and Scripts: Linguistic Evidence and Dating Tool
key_dimensions: Evolution: Greek legends (Indo-Greek) → bilingual Kharosthi-Greek → Brahmi-Prakrit → Sanskrit (Gupta) — Sanskritization trend
Brahmi script first appearing on coins under Ashoka vs. Kharosthi in Northwest — regional script distribution
Gupta coins with Sanskrit legends — first systematic use of Sanskrit on coins, marking cultural shift
UPSC trap: Kharosthi on coins limited to Northwest India, Brahmi had pan-India distribution

concepts.name: Comparative Analysis: Coinage Gaps and What Absence of Coins Indicates
key_dimensions: No coins from Vedic period — debate on barter vs. Nishka/Satamana as proto-money
Absence of Harappan coins despite advanced urban economy — implication for monetization theories
Sparse coinage in early Gupta period followed by explosion — what triggers monetization phases
UPSC trap: Absence of coins ≠ absence of trade; use of alternative media (grain, cloth, cowries)

concepts.name: Numismatics as Historiographical Method: Contribution to Reconstructing Ancient History
key_dimensions: Coins as the ONLY source for certain rulers (many Indo-Greek kings known only from coins)
Fixing dynastic chronology using coin stratigraphy — Cunningham's methodology and its limitations
Coin hoards and their archaeological context — what hoards indicate about political instability periods
Limitations of coins as source: Propaganda, selective iconography, and forged coins in ancient times (Arthashastra mentions this)
